teaser.text: American Electric Power (AEP) is an electric utility: it sells electricity, the ability to supply it when needed, and access to the wires that carry it. The dollar comes in through regulated bills, wholesale contracts and market sales, then goes out to fuel, workers, maintenance, financing and construction.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for AEP?

paragraphs.text: The bear case assumes contracted demand converts slowly while AEP builds ahead of customers. Delayed recovery, affordability pressure, debt and equity issuance weaken earnings per share and compress the multiple. The price falls from $102.55 in October 2027 to $89.56 by October 2029. Its 30% probability reflects capital spending above operating cash and debt of $52,836 million, but regulated assets prevent this from becoming a collapse scenario.

The bull case assumes large-load projects energize on schedule, transmission investment enters service and regulators allow timely recovery. Better cash generation limits dilution, earnings reach the upper end of guidance and the multiple expands gradually. The price rises from $130.47 to $164.24. Its 20% probability reflects the real upside from contracted load and rate-base growth, but execution must succeed across customers, construction and regulation.

blocks.heading: How much cash does AEP really make?

paragraphs.text: Stock-based compensation is another claim on shareholders. Employees receive value even when the company does not pay that value in cash immediately, and future share issuance can dilute existing owners. The specialist therefore asks whether operating cash will cover construction, dividends and debt service without repeated external financing.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for AEP today?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, tells investors how much they pay for each dollar of profit. AEP’s forward P/E is lower than its trailing P/E because the price assumes earnings will grow. The forward multiple uses adjusted operating earnings, which exclude items management considers unrelated to ongoing performance. The judgment still depends on whether regulators allow AEP to recover its costs and earn a return.

dividend.meta_description: AEP's dividend, cash coverage, planned increases, risks and yield are explained in plain English.
dividend.opening: AEP currently pays $0.95 per quarter per share, while operating cash remains below capital spending. AEP's dividend sits alongside construction, debt service and the need for outside financing.
dividend.closing: The full AEP memo also covers AEP's business, rivals, management plans and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does AEP pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise modestly in the base case from the current $0.95 quarterly rate to $3.88, $3.96 and $4.04 across the forecast windows. The increases follow the recent $0.02 quarterly step and management’s 50%–60% payout target. The bear case freezes annual dividends at $3.80 because debt and construction needs remain high; the bull case reaches $3.96, $4.12 and $4.28 because stronger earnings support faster increases.

blocks.heading: Does AEP's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Dividends remained a continuing claim on cash, while AEP used no share buybacks in the years shown. The money therefore bought a more regulated asset base and more generating capacity, but it did not yet prove that the returns will outweigh the financing burden. AEP’s plan has advanced; whether it works will be decided by the earnings those assets produce over time.

Stock-based compensation is another claim on shareholders. Employees receive value even when the company does not pay that value in cash immediately, and future share issuance can dilute existing owners. The specialist therefore asks whether operating cash will cover construction, dividends and debt service without repeated external financing.

blocks.heading: What has AEP guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management promises annual operating-earnings growth of 7%–9% through 2030. It expects a compound annual growth rate greater than 9% through 2030, based on the 2025 guidance midpoint. Operating EPS is its selected measure of recurring performance; GAAP earnings also include items such as impairments or asset-sale effects. A higher annual target after the first half of 2026 matters only if ordinary utility operations can support it.

AEP expects rate base to grow nearly 11% annually through 2030. It targets a 50%–60% payout ratio and a 10%–13% total annual shareholder return, but projects must still be approved, completed and placed in rates.

blocks.heading: Has AEP kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Trade coverage put Fehrman’s compensation at $36.6 million in 2025. It attributed $29.3 million to stock awards. AEP also aims to execute a $78 billion five-year capital plan and reiterated annual operating-earnings growth of 7%–9% on its Q2 2026 call. Those are targets, not delivered results. Shareholders can vote on pay, but AEP’s say-on-pay vote is advisory and cannot force the board to change the plan.

The fairest verdict is not that AEP’s leaders are automatically on shareholders’ side, or against them. It is that investors must watch whether independent directors challenge management, whether new financing earns its cost, and whether pay follows reliable performance rather than promises.

blocks.heading: What has AEP's revenue and profit trend been?

paragraphs.text: Revenue increased in the second quarter of 2026, while reported net income and diluted EPS fell. The comparison is distorted because the 2025 quarter included the $499 million FERC-related benefit connected largely with earlier years.
